item.title: A new reason for magic numbers: Scientists discover the secret behind an unusually stable molecular cluster
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, technical detail

A new reason for magic numbers: Scientists discover the secret behind an unusually stable molecular cluster

Why are some groups of molecules remarkably stable while others readily break apart? Researchers at Bar-Ilan University have discovered a surprising explanation for why clusters containing exactly six molecules of glycine, the simplest amino acid, are exceptionally stable—making six a "magic number." Moreover, they have uncovered the reason for this increased stability. The secret lies in a transformation that takes place when the molecules come together: they change their structure and become zwitterions, allowing them to form stronger bonds with one another.

The discovery sheds new light on how molecules interact and organize themselves, offering a new perspective on the chemistry of amino acids and the early molecular processes associated with the origins of life.

Published in the Journal of Chemical Physics, the study combines laboratory experiments with advanced computer simulations to investigate how glycine molecules (and amino acids in general) assemble into clusters.

The study was led by Michal Roth, a Ph.D. student working with Yoni Toker from the Department of Physics at Bar-Ilan University and Dan Thomas Major from the Department of Chemistry at Bar-Ilan University. Combining laboratory mass spectrometry experiments with advanced computational modeling and molecular dynamics simulations, the team investigated how glycine molecules assemble and what makes certain clusters exceptionally stable.

"Magic numbers are a well-known phenomenon that has always fascinated me," says Toker. "I was therefore very surprised when my student discovered a new source for magic numbers that has not been reported before."

Why six? The surprising chemistry behind molecular stability

Scientists have long observed that clusters containing certain numbers of molecules are much more abundant than others. These particularly stable groupings are known as "magic number" clusters. Until now, their unusual stability has generally been explained by the way molecules arrange themselves: magic numbers occur when the number of molecules in the clusters exactly corresponds to forming especially symmetrical and stable structures.

The Bar-Ilan researchers discovered a different explanation for the six-molecule glycine cluster. Glycine, like other amino acids, can exist in different electrical forms. The form usually drawn in textbooks is known as the neutral form. However, by changing the position of one proton, one can arrive at another form, known as a zwitterion. In this form, one end of the molecule is positively charged while the other is negatively charged.

While this charged arrangement is energetically unfavorable for a single glycine molecule in the gas phase, zwitterions bind more strongly to each other, and therefore it is expected that for larger clusters the molecules will change to their zwitterionic structure. The researchers found that this transition is abrupt: in clusters with five or fewer molecules, the molecules are in their neutral form, while in the hexamer, all the molecules switch to their zwitterionic form.

Computer simulations showed just how dramatic the difference is: the six-molecule cluster had a calculated dissociation temperature of approximately 1,200 kelvin, compared with approximately 450 kelvin for a cluster of five molecules and 480 kelvin for one containing seven molecules. In other words, the six-molecule cluster can withstand far higher temperatures before breaking apart.

What does this mean for understanding the origins of life?

Glycine is of particular interest to scientists studying the origins of life. It is the simplest amino acid, one of the building blocks of proteins, and has also been detected in meteorites, asteroids and comets. Indeed, in this detection, glycine had the highest abundance of all amino acids.

Understanding how amino acid molecules interact, bond and organize themselves is an important part of investigating the chemistry that preceded life. The discovery that six glycine molecules can undergo a collective electrical transformation and form an unusually stable structure provides a new example of how interactions between molecules can produce properties that individual molecules do not possess.

While the study does not directly examine the formation of proteins or peptides, its findings could help researchers better understand the molecular interactions that may have played a role in the early stages of their formation.

The researchers now hope to investigate whether other amino acids undergo similar transformations when they form molecular clusters.

Publication details

Michal Roth First et al., Neutral-to-zwitterionic transition in protonated glycine clusters drives magic number stability, The Journal of Chemical Physics (2026). DOI: 10.1063/5.0350852

Journal information: Journal of Chemical Physics

Provided by Bar-Ilan University

item.title: Researchers reveal inner-core structural evolution of Typhoon Bavi using multisensor satellite observations
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: multisensor data, complex topic explained

Researchers reveal inner-core structural evolution of Typhoon Bavi using multisensor satellite observations

Tropical cyclones frequently undergo rapid, complex structural changes within their inner cores, such as eyewall replacement and wind-field expansion, that strongly influence typhoon intensity and coastal hazards. However, capturing these multilayered transformations continuously from the ocean surface to the upper cloud tops remains a major observational challenge.

To address this challenge, a research team from the Institute of Oceanology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (IOCAS) reconstructed the full inner-core structural evolution of Typhoon Bavi by integrating 17 repeated spaceborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR) overpasses with geostationary infrared imagery and synthetic microwave brightness temperature fields.

Their findings were published in the Journal of Remote Sensing on Nov. 11.

Tracking the typhoon across vertical layers

To track the typhoon across multiple vertical levels simultaneously, the researchers combined near-surface ocean wind fields derived from NOAA/STAR tropical cyclone SAR products with cloud-top center positions identified from the Japan Meteorological Agency's Himawari-9 infrared observations. In addition, they generated hourly synthetic 89-GHz microwave brightness temperature fields from multispectral infrared measurements to monitor deep convection and eyewall reorganization around the typhoon's eye.

These integrated satellite observations uncovered a clear temporal sequence in how the typhoon's inner core reorganized: A secondary eyewall formed and contracted inward first, followed by a pronounced horizontal separation between the near-surface circulation center and the upper-level cloud-top center. Finally, the typhoon's strong-wind region expanded substantially during its weakening stage.

"Coordinated multisensor observations provide a rare vertical cross section of a typhoon's life cycle," said Dr. Mu Shanshan, first author of the study. By pairing repeated high-resolution SAR wind snapshots with continuous geostationary infrared and synthetic microwave tracking, the researchers can pinpoint the exact timing of eyewall replacement, vertical vortex tilt and near-surface wind broadening.

Eyewall replacement precedes growing vortex tilt

Between 00:00 UTC on July 5 and July 6, the synthetic 89-GHz imagery captured the formation, intensification and inward contraction of the outer eyewall, showing that the eyewall replacement cycle concluded around 23:00 UTC on July 6.

During the initial formation of the secondary eyewall, the horizontal offset between the near-surface circulation center and the infrared cloud-top center (defined as the SAR–IR tilt) was relatively small at roughly 5 to 10 km (3 to 6 miles). As the replacement process neared completion, this offset widened to 17.8 km (11.1 miles) and further increased to 20.8 km (12.9 miles) in observations on July 7.

Weaker winds spread over a wider area

High-resolution SAR wind retrievals further revealed that as Typhoon Bavi weakened in its later stages, its maximum near-surface wind speed declined overall while its radius of maximum wind (RMW) expanded dramatically. During the typhoon's peak intensity phase, the RMW was tightly concentrated between 15 and 26 km (9 and 16 miles). In subsequent multiscene observations, however, the RMW stretched beyond 100 km (62 miles) and exceeded 200 km (124 miles) in individual overpasses, demonstrating a marked outward broadening of the gale-force wind swath.

"Understanding when and how a typhoon's wind field expands is just as critical for disaster preparedness as forecasting peak wind speed," said Dr. Wang Chong, corresponding author of the study.

This observational case provides a valuable benchmark for studying the physical coupling between eyewall replacement cycles, cross-layer center displacement and outer wind-field growth.

More information

Shanshan Mu et al., Repeated Spaceborne SAR and Multisensor Observations of Tropical-Cyclone Inner-Core Structural Evolution, Journal of Remote Sensing (2026). DOI: 10.34133/remotesensing.1095

item.title: Earth’s Water May Have Formed in This Fiery Furnace
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original hypothesis, technical detail

It’s one of the most fundamental questions about life on Earth: How did water get here?

One possibility is that it was delivered as frozen ice by a bombardment of meteorites smashing into our planet’s surface. Another is that the chemistry of the early Earth somehow produced water from molten rock—a theory that’s the focus of a new study published in Nature Geoscience.

The researchers behind the hypothesis are calling it “pebble rain” (or “pebble accretion”). What happens is silicate rocks with iron inside, drawn toward Earth by its increasing mass and gravitational pull, react with hydrogen in the atmosphere. Given the high speeds, high pressure, and high volume of incoming rocks involved, the subsequent chemical reactions could have stripped away the oxygen from the iron in the pebble showers, releasing water vapor as a by-product.

The researchers estimate that around 200 oceans’ worth of H2O may have been released in this way, supplying the planet with the magic ingredient for life. These pebbles would have been external visitors, like meteorites, but the water would’ve been formed on Earth rather than in space.

What’s more, the same process could plausibly happen on other planets as they form too—opening up new possibilities in our search for extraterrestrial life. “Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites,” study author Zachary Sharp explained in a statement. “Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism.”

The researchers simulated the conditions of the early Earth in their lab with temperatures of up to 2,552°F, and heating silicate rocks in streams of hydrogen. Almost 80 percent of the iron oxide in the samples turned into metallic iron, producing water vapor along the way.

“Looking out over a large body of water, it’s hard to imagine that that water may have been produced four-and-a-half billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere,” Sharp said, “but it very well may have.”

Lead Image: University of New Mexico

item.title: How Streams Breathe: The Science of Expanding and Contracting
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: technical detail, clear explanation

Editors’ Highlights are summaries of recent papers by AGU’s journal editors.

Stream networks are highly dynamic, constantly breathing by contraction and expansion, resulting in changing stream lengths. This is highly relevant for nutrient transport and greenhouse gas emissions. The interconnection of stream discharge and stream length, also termed elasticity, has been determined by measurements in small catchments experimentally and extrapolated by applying empirical power law models.

Rathore et al. [2026] demonstrate the limits of these laws using integrating modeling and a unique observational dataset. They also propose a novel asynchronous peak scaling approach which appears to be universal and provides a robust framework across scales from small to large watersheds. More importantly, the authors are able to mechanistically explain their findings from the physics-based simulations, which is highly satisfactory and lends confidence in the results.

Citation: Rathore, S. S., Gomez‐Velez, J. D., Herndon, E. M., & Painter, S. L. (2026).Hysteretic dynamics of stream network expansion and contraction revealed through high‐resolution integrated hydrological modeling. Water Resources Research, 62, e2025WR042993. https://doi.org/10.1029/2025WR042993

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: historical significance, technical detail

On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets, the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched.

Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space. (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control.

Why it mattered

Billed as the "most successful sounding rocket of the space age," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so.

"The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview. "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds."

While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach space, many more made successful launches in the decades that followed.

Engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that launched two Phillipine monkeys on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for human spaceflight.

More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have launched since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

item.title: Mindfulness training may bring out the worst in some employees
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, clear explanation

Mindfulness training may bring out the worst in some employees

Contrary to popular belief, mindfulness training in the workplace can make some employees angrier and more likely to treat coworkers with disrespect.

According to the Harvard Business Review, more than half of large companies offer some form of mindfulness training, often promoted as a way to make employees calmer, kinder and more considerate of others.

But a new study from the University of South Florida, published in the Journal of Business Ethics, reveals a surprising catch: mindfulness training can backfire, depending on the personalities of employees who undergo it.

"Mindfulness training makes us more aware of our thoughts and feelings, but that doesn't necessarily make us better people," said Adam Kay, the study's author and assistant professor in the School of Management at USF's Muma College of Business.

What comes into focus may differ from person to person. For Machiavellian employees, who tend to be manipulative and contemptuous of others, Kay suggests that mindfulness training can heighten their awareness of negative feelings they already harbor, with troubling implications for how they treat coworkers.

To investigate, Kay recruited 600 health care workers for a monthlong field experiment, randomly assigning them to mindfulness training, breathwork or a waitlist control. Results showed that Machiavellian employees who underwent mindfulness training experienced heightened feelings of contempt, anger and disgust toward their coworkers, which they then channeled into workplace incivility.

"Workplace incivility isn't always obvious," Kay said. "It usually involves subtle acts of disrespect that are easy to dismiss or deny—but that doesn't make it harmless." Indeed, the Society for Human Resource Management estimates that workplace incivility costs U.S. employers more than $2 billion each day in lost productivity and absenteeism.

"That workplace incivility can be so damaging yet so difficult to pin on perpetrators may be precisely why it appeals to Machiavellians, who tend to be calculating and reputation-conscious," Kay said.

In line with this reasoning, the study found that Machiavellians who underwent mindfulness training engaged in more subtle forms of mistreatment—such as being rude or dismissive—but not in more blatant forms of misconduct, such as publicly embarrassing coworkers.

Kay cautioned that these findings are not a reason for organizations to abandon mindfulness training. Instead, they underscore the importance of considering how different employees respond to mindfulness programs and evaluating not only their intended benefits but also their potential costs.

"Mindfulness training can bring our darker feelings into sharper focus," Kay said. "And sometimes, it's our coworkers who pay the price."

Publication details

Adam A. Kay, The Dark Side of Mindfulness at Work: How Mindfulness Training Enlivens Machiavellian Incivility, Journal of Business Ethics (2026). DOI: 10.1007/s10551-026-06513-3

Journal information: Journal of Business Ethics

Provided by University of South Florida

item.title: 'Blade Runner 2099' executive producers talk architectural easter eggs and franchise continuity for Prime Video's new sci-fi series (interview)
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original content, clear explanation

Prime Video's new "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising.

This dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, "Blade Runner." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.

Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret.

We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel.

"When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over."

"Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo.

"We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so new fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion."

Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced.

"Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey."

With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of "Blade Runner 2099's" 8-episode season.

"You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner.

"There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.”

"Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

item.title: Medieval chain mail discovered during underwater excavation of 15th-century 'floating castle' that sank off Sweden
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: historical significance, technical detail

Medieval chain mail discovered during underwater excavation of 15th-century 'floating castle' that sank off Sweden

A 15th-century shipwreck is yielding clues to the medieval tragedy that destroyed Griffin, King Hans's "floating castle."

Archaeologists have recovered high-quality chain mail armor from the 15th-century wreck of Gribshunden or Griffin, a royal warship that doubled as a "floating castle" for King Hans of Denmark. The ship exploded and sank in 1495, but maritime archaeologists have just begun exploring the area beneath the forecastle, an elevated combat platform at the front of the ship, where they discovered the armor and a unique munitions chest.

The chain mail was, "rather surprisingly, completely exposed," Rolf Warming, an archaeologist at Stockholm University and lead investigator of the Griffin project in collaboration with Södertörn University, told Live Science in an email. "It was only by chance that we came across it, and it shows just how much is still on the wreck site."

The mail armor was made of copper alloy and was found in a part of the ship that may have been used as a storage area for military gear, according to a Nov. 24 statement. "Historical sources indicate that German mercenaries, or Landsknechts, were aboard Griffin when it sank in 1495," Rodrigo Pacheco-Ruiz, an archaeologist at the University of Southampton in the U.K. who is the co-investigator on the project, said in the statement. The mercenaries may have stored their armor in the area, "although we've yet to establish a precise function for the space," Pacheco-Ruiz said.

The 15th-century warship was rediscovered in the Baltic Sea off the south coast of Sweden in the 1970s but formally identified by archaeologists as Griffin in 2013.

Griffin was the flagship of the naval fleet of King Hans of Denmark and Norway. In 1495, Hans was sailing to Kalmar in Sweden to negotiate a political alliance and force Sweden back into a union with Denmark and Norway. He had brought with him around 150 German mercenary soldiers. "It was important to demonstrate military prowess, and the German and Swiss mercenaries were the finest you could get at that time," Warming told Live Science.

During a stop at the port of Ronneby in what is now Sweden, Griffin caught fire, perhaps after being struck by lightning, and sank. Eyewitnesses who escaped reported that many men died in the tragic event. King Hans, however, was onshore when the warship sank.

The warship has been well-preserved over the centuries thanks to the low salinity of the Baltic waters and the lack of shipworms, marine mollusks also known as the "termites of the sea" because of the damage they do to wood.

The chain mail recovered in October is of exceptionally high quality, Warming said in the statement, but it was not necessarily the armor of an elite knight. "This kind of armour could remain in use for extended periods, often undergoing repairs or being reused, so these fragments may represent older military equipment that was still active," he said.

But the researchers discovered more than just the chain mail.

"This year's campaign was an unusually exciting investigation!" The team found a unique munitions chest called a "zeuglade" in German. "We have taken different samples to try to determine the contents of the chest and perhaps find traces of gunpowder," Warming said. The chest may have belonged to the German mercenaries who were aboard.

"It was in the process of documenting the chest that I unexpectedly discovered exposed mail-armour fragments in the vicinity of the chest, along other items that could indicate more chests," Warming added. "This leads us to believe this may have been a stowage area, located just beneath the forecastle."

Warming said that the research team is currently using chemical analysis to investigate the origins of the armor and the chest to learn more about medieval military matters.

"It is probable that the mail armour belongs to the mercenaries, but it could also belong to someone else," Warming said. "The chest might also belong to them, but we don't know yet.
